newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-DOWNHILLER LINDH KEEPS AMERICA ON TOP.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-DOWNHILLER LINDH KEEPS AMERICA ON TOP.

text.p: Hilary Lindh of the United States won the women's downhill gold medal at the Alpine skiing world championships on Saturday, continuing a north American tradition.
Lindh, who has not finished in the top three of any World Cup race this season, started 14th and stunned the favourites with a time of one minute 41.18 seconds.
The American was pretty surprised too. "I'm just in shock right now," she said at the finish.

Switzerland's Heidi Zurbriggen took the silver medal in 1:41.24 and Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg, a double world champion at the last championships in 1996 but without a medal here before Saturday, was delighted with the bronze in 1:41.44.

It was the Swede's first medal in a speed discipline after winning five golds in technical and combined events and she said she was proud of her achievement. It was also the first time she has won anything other than a gold.
The race was run in mostly brilliant sunshine, a welcome change after snow and wind disrupted the last two days.
Isolde Kostner, winner of the super-G this week, finished a close fourth and struggled to hide her disappointment in failing to continue Italy's streak of three golds in three races.

Lindh, the 1992 Olympic downhill silver medallist who last won a race in 1994, followed in the wake of 1996 downhill champion and compatriot Picabo Street -- who is absent this year due to injury -- and 1993 champion Kate Pace of Canada.
The last European to win the women's downhill title was Austrian Petra Kronberger in Saalbach in 1991.

"I thought maybe I could win a medal but I didn't know I could be first," said the 27-year-old Lindh, who won a bronze in the discipline last year in Sierra Nevada although she had not been on the podium all season before that race either.
"I guess when I race big events I get excited," she said.
Lindh had spent a couple of months mulling over her future at the end of last season and opted to continue although probably only for one further year on the circuit.
"I was so close to not racing this year," she said. "Even at the start of the season I didn't know if I had made the right decision."
She had a good run in training but was never regarded as one of the likely medallists on the hill.
The unexpected victory will probably ensure that Lindh now stays on the circuit for the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics in Japan.
But Lindh said she would take time out to decide over the spring.
"As far as next year is concerned it's all up in the air at this point. I'm not sure," she said.
Zurbriggen, who has won two World Cup downhills this season, had looked like she was going to restore the European supremacy but she failed at the last moment.
"I felt I was really fast today," said the sister of the great all-rounder Pirmin Zurbriggen.
"At some points my skis were so fast it was difficult to control them. I also noticed I was jumping a long way. I made a mistake on the last turn when I think I lost the race."
Germany's Katja Seizinger, starting off what is sure to be a gruelling day with the women's combined downhill following after the regular downhill, lost time on a final jump and finished fifth.
